title: India and Nine Partners Sign San Francisco Declaration to Protect AI Supply Chains
excerpt: The Pax Silica signatories agreed common definitions for the sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure behind AI, and five working groups to act on them — a declaration of shared understanding, not yet a rulebook.
body:
• India and nine other governments signed the San Francisco Declaration on November 15, agreeing that safeguarding the technologies and infrastructure behind AI supply chains is a "shared endeavour."
  • The declaration sets common definitions for two asset classes — sensitive technologies, and the critical infrastructure from ports to digital platforms that AI supply chains run on — and proposes five working groups to carry the work forward.
  • It is a declaration, not a rulebook: the text sets no deadlines, penalties or common export rules, and it does not name China, though it was framed by participants against competition with China over advanced technology.
  • For India, the value is a seat in the group defining what counts as a trusted AI supply chain while it builds domestic semiconductor and computing capacity.

India has joined nine other governments in a joint declaration to protect the supply chains that advanced artificial intelligence depends on. The San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity was signed on November 15 at the Pax Silica Founders Retreat in San Francisco, convened by US Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob Helberg, according to the US State Department, which released the full text.

Who signed, and what they agreed

"One quirk of the text needs translating: it speaks throughout of "super intelligence" (SI) supply chains rather than AI."

The ten signatories are the United States, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the United Arab Emirates and the United Kingdom. The declaration affirms that economic security is fundamental to national security, and that resilience is best achieved by reducing excessive dependencies through diversified and trusted supply chains. It also commits the participants to coordinated efforts against economic coercion, supply-chain disruptions and non-market practices that distort markets, and to cooperation on enforcing their respective policies against undue access to, influence over, or control of the assets it covers.

The core of the text is a pair of shared definitions. "Sensitive technologies" are the goods, software, materials, knowledge, components and inputs used to produce them, and their means of production, essential to AI supply chains — defined by the harm their theft, illicit transfer or acquisition by hostile actors could cause, including a meaningful military or intelligence advantage or undue economic leverage. "Critical infrastructure" is the physical and digital systems those supply chains depend on: ports, terminals, transport, communications and logistics networks, the information-technology and energy infrastructure behind them, and the digital platforms that coordinate them.

Five working groups, no rulebook yet

To carry the declaration into practice, the signatories resolved to establish working groups in five areas: pro-innovation policy frameworks, AI adoption in key sectors, supply chain cooperation across the AI stack, safe harbours and supply chain security hubs, and AI security and resilience. The State Department describes this as Pax Silica — the US-led initiative launched in December last year to secure supply chains for silicon and other minerals essential to semiconductors and AI — entering a new phase, in which the coalition "cements its shared principles into a working partnership with a common baseline and a path to act on it."

Readers should be clear about what the declaration is not. The text released by the ten governments contains no deadlines, no penalties and no common rules on exports or investment screening; its operative verbs are recognising, affirming and declaring a common understanding. It also never names China. The competitive framing comes from the participants and the coverage around the signing: the Hindu BusinessLine reported the declaration as treating AI supply-chain protection as a shared endeavour "amid growing competition with China in emerging technology," and Reuters described the pact as part of Washington's push to build allied economic-security architecture as competition with Beijing over frontier technologies intensifies.

Terminology, and what comes next

One quirk of the text needs translating: it speaks throughout of "super intelligence" (SI) supply chains rather than AI. The US government uses that term after President Donald Trump signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence, and the declaration's own footnote notes that for some participants, "super intelligence" refers to artificial intelligence. The substance is the AI stack — chips, the minerals and equipment behind them, and the infrastructure that moves and powers them.

For India, participation puts it inside the group setting the baseline definitions at a moment when it is expanding domestic semiconductor manufacturing and advanced computing while trying to reduce reliance on foreign sources for components and equipment, as Inc42 noted in its report. Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden are expected to sign in the coming days, the Financial Times reported. What would convert the declaration from definitions into obligations — joint lists of protected technologies, common screening practices, dated working-group outputs — has not been published; the working groups' first deliverables are the marker to watch.
nri_angle: India's seat in the Pax Silica group shapes the trusted-supply-chain rules that Indian and Indian-American technology firms, chip designers and data-centre operators will build under.
